q: בת 85, עצמאית ב- BADL וללא חסר קוגניטיבי. ברקע אוסטאופורוזיס, מטופלת בויטמין D ו- ALENDRONATE. בנוסף, יתר לחץ דם שעד כה טופל עם דיאטה ופעילות גופנית, ללא טיפול תרופתי. בחודשים האחרונים מדידות חוזרות של לחצי דם סביב 165/90. מהי הגישה הטיפולית המתאימה בחולה זו?
o: המטופלת עם סיכון קרדיו-וסקולרי נמוך. אין צורך בטיפול להורדת לחצי הדם
הימנעות מטיפול ב- HYDOCHLOROTHIASIDE עקב אוסטאופורוזיס
טיפול ב- DOXAZOCIN (CADEX) כקו ראשון
טיפול ב- AMLODIPINE (AMLO) כקו ראשון
explanation:
**Antihypertensive treatment** is selected according to patient characteristics, efficacy and adverse effects. Long-acting calcium channel blockers are effective in older adults; reduced peripheral resistance and lack of significant central or metabolic effects fit this population (Hazzard pp. 1224–1226). The historical JNC8 target is retained as historical context, not as a current individualized target (James et al., JAMA 2014, p. 507).
"BP goal of less than 150/90 mm Hg" (James et al., p. 507).

**A. Low cardiovascular risk; no blood-pressure treatment is needed.** Wrong, repeated pressure remains elevated despite lifestyle changes. The source describes drug treatment when lifestyle measures fail to achieve the target; the stem does not justify withholding therapy on the basis of low risk (p. 1225).
**B. Avoid hydrochlorothiazide because of osteoporosis.** Wrong, osteoporosis is not a reason to avoid a thiazide: Table 79-4 lists improved bone mineral density as a benefit. Selection still requires consideration of adverse effects and individual characteristics (pp. 1225–1226).
**C. Doxazosin (Cadex) as first-line therapy.** Wrong, alpha blockers can cause postural hypotension and were associated with more heart-failure admissions than a diuretic. The book largely limits monotherapy to men who may benefit for prostatic symptoms, which does not fit this patient (p. 1226).
**D. Amlodipine (Amlo) as first-line therapy.** Correct, the officially accepted choice. Long-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are supported in older hypertensive adults. Initiate cautiously and adapt treatment and targets to response and tolerability; acceptance does not establish that this is all the treatment required (pp. 1225–1226).

Official answer: D. The 85-year-old patient with repeated readings of 165/90 requires pharmacologic treatment: these readings exceed the historical target cited in the explanation, generally below 150/90, although the target depends on clinical context. Amlodipine, a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, is the accepted option. The source supports long-acting calcium channel blockers in older adults and selection according to patient characteristics (Hazzard pp. 1224–1226; James et al., p. 507).

The historical-target note is retained and is not an instruction for a current individual target.

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1224–1226, Table 79-4; James PA et al. 2014 Evidence-Based Guideline for the Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults. JAMA. 2014;311:507–520, p. 507. doi:10.1001/jama.2013.284427.

q: A 77-year-old man takes hydrochlorothiazide, but his blood pressure remains uncontrolled. A switch to chlorthalidone is being considered. Which difference does Hazzard identify?
o: Chlorthalidone has greater potency and a longer half-life
Chlorthalidone has greater potency and a shorter half-life
Chlorthalidone has lower potency and a longer half-life
Chlorthalidone has lower potency and a shorter half-life
explanation:
**Chlorthalidone** is the recommended drug within the thiazide class in this source (p. 1225). In addition to trial evidence of efficacy, "it has greater potency and a longer half-life than hydrochlorothiazide" (p. 1225).

**A. Chlorthalidone has greater potency and a longer half-life.** Correct, both properties are stated as considerations favoring chlorthalidone within the thiazide class (p. 1225).
**B. Chlorthalidone has greater potency and a shorter half-life.** Wrong, the greater potency is supported, but its half-life is longer rather than shorter (p. 1225).
**C. Chlorthalidone has lower potency and a longer half-life.** Wrong, the longer half-life is supported, but chlorthalidone has greater rather than lower potency (p. 1225).
**D. Chlorthalidone has lower potency and a shorter half-life.** Wrong, neither property matches the source: chlorthalidone has greater potency and a longer half-life (p. 1225).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1225.

q: An older man taking an alpha blocker for hypertension reports dizziness on standing. Which property of this drug class is relevant to assessment?
o: A tendency to produce postural hypotension.
A tendency to protect against postural hypotension.
Fewer heart-failure admissions than thiazide-type diuretic monotherapy.
Preferred monotherapy for uncomplicated hypertension in older adults.
explanation:
**Alpha-1 receptor antagonists** have a "predilection to produce postural hypotension" (p. 1226). This is relevant to symptoms on standing. The source also reports greater heart-failure hospitalization risk than diuretic monotherapy and consequently limits their role as initial monotherapy (p. 1226).

**A. A tendency to produce postural hypotension.** Correct, the stated tendency to cause postural hypotension fits the symptom being assessed, without proving drug causation (p. 1226).
**B. A tendency to protect against postural hypotension.** Wrong, the source describes production of postural hypotension, not protection against it (p. 1226).
**C. Fewer heart-failure admissions than thiazide-type diuretic monotherapy.** Wrong, the trial comparison showed higher rather than lower heart-failure hospitalization risk with alpha-blocker monotherapy (p. 1226).
**D. Preferred monotherapy for uncomplicated hypertension in older adults.** Wrong, the source limits monotherapy to selected men with beneficial effects on prostatic symptoms rather than preferring it broadly for uncomplicated hypertension (p. 1226).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1226.

q: An 81-year-old ambulatory woman has uncontrolled hypertension and needs a treatment adjustment. Which principle should guide initiation and dose titration in older adults according to Hazzard?
o: Start at a reduced dose and increase gradually according to tolerability
Start at an increased dose and increase gradually according to tolerability
Start at a reduced dose and increase rapidly despite dizziness
Start at an increased dose and increase rapidly despite dizziness
explanation:
**Reduced starting doses** and gradual titration are the source's general prescribing approach for older patients with hypertension. It states that "the starting dose should be reduced in older patients and dosage titration be carried out gradually" (p. 1225). Adverse effects such as postural hypotension limit aggressive treatment, so tolerability matters during escalation (p. 1225).

**A. Start at a reduced dose and increase gradually according to tolerability.** Correct, both the initial dose and the pace of titration match the stated approach; monitoring tolerability also respects the warning about adverse effects (p. 1225).
**B. Start at an increased dose and increase gradually according to tolerability.** Wrong, gradual titration does not correct the excessive starting dose: the source recommends reducing the initial dose in older patients (p. 1225).
**C. Start at a reduced dose and increase rapidly despite dizziness.** Wrong, the reduced starting dose is appropriate, but rapid escalation despite dizziness ignores the gradual-titration and adverse-effect precautions (p. 1225).
**D. Start at an increased dose and increase rapidly despite dizziness.** Wrong, an increased starting dose and rapid escalation both conflict with the recommended approach; dizziness should not be disregarded during intensification (p. 1225).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1225.

q: A 76-year-old woman treated for hypertension reports dizziness on standing. Which measurement principle is important before changing treatment?
o: Use seated blood pressure to assess the response to standing
Use a high office reading to justify intensifying medication
Obtain supine and standing readings to detect a postural decrease
Use diastolic blood pressure in place of standing measurements
explanation:
**Supine and standing blood pressure** readings identify a postural decrease. Hazzard notes that postural hypotension is associated with falls and may be exacerbated by almost all antihypertensive medication classes, making its identification relevant during treatment. (p. 1222)
"always obtain supine and upright standing readings to determine if there is evidence for an orthostatic or postural decrease in blood pressure." (p. 1222)
"The presence of postural hypotension is an important risk factor for falls and may be exacerbated by almost all antihypertensive medication classes." (p. 1222)

**A. Use seated blood pressure to assess the response to standing.** Wrong, a seated reading does not provide the supine-to-standing comparison required to assess the reported positional symptoms. (p. 1222)
**B. Use a high office reading to justify intensifying medication.** Wrong, a high office reading does not establish the standing response; the source calls for postural measurements throughout treatment. (p. 1222)
**C. Obtain supine and standing readings to detect a postural decrease.** Correct, these measurements directly implement the recommended assessment for a postural fall in pressure. (p. 1222)
**D. Use diastolic blood pressure in place of standing measurements.** Wrong, focusing on diastolic pressure does not replace the paired positional measurements needed to detect a postural decrease. (p. 1222)

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., p. 1222.

q: A 78-year-old man with diabetes and chronic kidney disease is having his hypertension treatment reviewed. How should the treatment goal be set according to Hazzard?
o: Apply a uniform age-based target despite differences in function and comorbidity
Use a single blood pressure reading as the basis for diagnosis and treatment
Individualize the target for comorbidity, risk, and quality of life
Pursue the lowest achievable pressure despite treatment-related postural symptoms
explanation:
**Individualized blood pressure goals** reflect the heterogeneity of older adults with multimorbidity and frailty. Treatment should limit adverse effects and harm to quality of life; postural hypotension can require modification of the target (p. 1223).
"it is important to establish individualized patient treatment goals utilizing therapies that are least likely to produce adverse side effects or have a negative impact on quality of life." (p. 1223).
"a hypertension diagnosis should never be based on a single elevated measurement." (p. 1219).

**A. Apply a uniform age-based target despite differences in function and comorbidity.** Wrong, the chapter describes the difficulty of one-size-fits-all targets in a heterogeneous population (p. 1223).
**B. Use a single blood pressure reading as the basis for diagnosis and treatment.** Wrong, the diagnosis requires repeated measurements rather than one elevated reading (p. 1219).
**C. Individualize the target for comorbidity, risk, and quality of life.** Correct, comorbidities influence the target, and the treatment-goal discussion explicitly includes adverse effects and quality of life (p. 1223).
**D. Pursue the lowest achievable pressure despite treatment-related postural symptoms.** Wrong, postural hypotension is a reason to reconsider the target, so the lowest achievable pressure is not the governing objective (p. 1223).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 1219, 1223.

q: An 81-year-old woman attends a routine visit without acute symptoms or evidence of acute target-organ injury. A single blood pressure measurement after walking to the clinic is higher than usual. What should be done before diagnosing sustained hypertension and changing treatment?
o: Base the diagnosis on the first elevated office measurement.
Use diastolic pressure as the principal guide to cardiovascular risk.
Use seated readings to avoid the influence of changes in posture.
Repeat standardized blood pressure measurements and arrange out-of-office monitoring.
explanation:
**Accurate repeated measurements** are essential because blood pressure is more variable in older people. Home or ambulatory monitoring can help evaluate an office-related elevation, while measurements in different postures identify an orthostatic decrease (p. 1222). "hypertension should never be diagnosed on the basis of a single blood pressure measurement" (p. 1222).

**A. Base the diagnosis on the first elevated office measurement.** Wrong, a single measurement is insufficient in a population with greater blood pressure variability; the diagnosis should use repeated measurements or home or ambulatory results (p. 1222).
**B. Use diastolic pressure as the principal guide to cardiovascular risk.** Wrong, Hazzard emphasizes the primacy of systolic over diastolic pressure for cardiovascular risk, so this proposed emphasis is misplaced (p. 1222).
**C. Use seated readings to avoid the influence of changes in posture.** Wrong, supine and standing readings are needed to look for an orthostatic decrease; avoiding posture changes misses that assessment (p. 1222).
**D. Repeat standardized blood pressure measurements and arrange out-of-office monitoring.** Correct, repeat measurements and home or ambulatory monitoring address variability and possible white coat hypertension before a sustained elevation is diagnosed (p. 1222).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1222.

q: An older man with hypertension and a previous myocardial infarction is being considered for a beta-blocker. Which consideration supports its use according to Hazzard?
o: Secondary prevention after a previous myocardial infarction
Its role as monotherapy for uncomplicated hypertension
Its role in reducing peripheral vascular resistance
Its role in preventing adverse metabolic effects
explanation:
**Beta-blocker selection** in older adults depends on a compelling indication. Hazzard reserves these drugs for indications including "secondary prevention for those patients who have had prior myocardial infarction" (p. 1226). It does not recommend beta-blocker monotherapy for uncomplicated hypertension in older patients (p. 1226).

**A. Secondary prevention after a previous myocardial infarction.** Correct, previous myocardial infarction is a stated compelling indication, so the drug has a role beyond treatment of uncomplicated hypertension (p. 1226).
**B. Its role as monotherapy for uncomplicated hypertension.** Wrong, Hazzard explicitly states that beta-blockers are not an appropriate monotherapy choice for older patients with uncomplicated hypertension (p. 1226).
**C. Its role in reducing peripheral vascular resistance.** Wrong, the table lists a possible increase in peripheral vascular resistance as a disadvantage, so the proposed vascular effect is not the stated reason to choose this class (p. 1226).
**D. Its role in preventing adverse metabolic effects.** Wrong, metabolic abnormalities are listed as a disadvantage of beta-blockers, rather than a benefit supporting selection (p. 1226).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1226.

q: An 85-year-old nursing-home resident with advanced Parkinson disease, dysphagia, recurrent aspiration pneumonia, and complete dependence for daily activities has persistently elevated blood pressure. His representative asks about treatment. Before selecting a drug, which approach follows Hazzard for a person with high comorbidity burden and limited life expectancy?
o: Choose a treatment target from age without discussing patient goals
Apply the community-living target before considering comorbidity burden
Individualize the treatment decision through clinical judgment and informed discussion
Select the drug formulation before considering adverse effects and quality of life
explanation:
**Individualized blood-pressure decisions** are needed when high comorbidity burden and limited life expectancy affect the balance of benefits and harms. The guidance quoted in Hazzard is to "utilize clinical judgment in a patient-informed discussion" (p. 1223). The page also emphasizes treatments least likely to impair quality of life; it does not establish that every such patient should remain untreated.

**A. Choose a treatment target from age without discussing patient goals.** Wrong, age alone omits the individualized discussion specified for this clinical context (p. 1223).
**B. Apply the community-living target before considering comorbidity burden.** Wrong, the source distinguishes ambulatory community-living adults from those with high comorbidity burden and limited life expectancy (p. 1223).
**C. Individualize the treatment decision through clinical judgment and informed discussion.** Correct, this matches the stated decision process and allows the eventual treatment plan to reflect goals and likely burdens (p. 1223).
**D. Select the drug formulation before considering adverse effects and quality of life.** Wrong, formulation does not replace first establishing individualized goals and considering adverse effects and quality of life (p. 1223).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1223.

q: A 76-year-old woman with hypertension and mild frailty walks with a walker and covers 5.2 meters in 8 seconds. Her baseline blood pressure is 148/82 on amlodipine 5 mg daily. In a trial she is assigned to an intensive systolic blood pressure target below 120 mm Hg. After amlodipine titration and addition of lisinopril, her blood pressure is 118/68 seated and 114/66 standing. She feels well and reports more energy. Which interpretation of the SPRINT evidence supports continuing her tolerated regimen with monitoring?
o: Benefits persisted in participants with frailty or impaired gait speed
Benefits diminished in participants with frailty or impaired gait speed
Injurious falls increased in participants assigned to intensive treatment
Quality of life declined in participants assigned to intensive treatment
explanation:
**Frailty did not negate the SPRINT benefit** reported in Hazzard: "These results did not differ for the most frail subgroup nor for those with impaired gait speed" (p. 1223). The source also reports no group difference in injurious falls or self-assessed health-related quality of life (p. 1223). Inference: her reported tolerability supports continued individualized monitoring rather than changing treatment because of frailty alone (p. 1223).

**A. Benefits persisted in participants with frailty or impaired gait speed.** Correct, the favorable cardiovascular and mortality findings did not differ in the most frail subgroup or in those with impaired gait speed (p. 1223).
**B. Benefits diminished in participants with frailty or impaired gait speed.** Wrong, the source explicitly reports that these results did not differ in either subgroup (p. 1223).
**C. Injurious falls increased in participants assigned to intensive treatment.** Wrong, the source reports no group difference in serious adverse events including injurious falls, although some other adverse events were higher (p. 1223).
**D. Quality of life declined in participants assigned to intensive treatment.** Wrong, the source reports no group difference in self-assessed health-related quality of life regardless of frailty status (p. 1223).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1223.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 1223, SPRINT

q: Chlorthalidone is being considered for hypertension in an older patient. How does Hazzard describe it in comparison with hydrochlorothiazide?
o: Lower potency and a shorter half-life
Greater potency and a longer half-life
Greater potency and a shorter half-life
Lower potency and a longer half-life
explanation:
**Chlorthalidone** is described as more potent and as having a longer half-life than hydrochlorothiazide. The source treats these as two separate characteristics; at equipotent doses, it reports a comparable incidence of hypokalemia (p. 1225).
"it has greater potency and a longer half-life than hydrochlorothiazide." (p. 1225).
"When equipotent doses are compared, the incidence of hypokalemia is comparable." (p. 1225).

**A. Lower potency and a shorter half-life.** Wrong, both features conflict with the comparison: chlorthalidone has greater potency and a longer half-life (p. 1225).
**B. Greater potency and a longer half-life.** Correct, both characteristics match the source comparison with hydrochlorothiazide (p. 1225).
**C. Greater potency and a shorter half-life.** Wrong, the potency comparison is supported, but the shorter half-life is not: chlorthalidone has a longer half-life (p. 1225).
**D. Lower potency and a longer half-life.** Wrong, the half-life comparison is supported, but the lower potency is not: chlorthalidone has greater potency (p. 1225).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1225.

q: A 73-year-old woman with hypertension takes a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug for joint pain. What is the role of reviewing this medication in her blood pressure evaluation?
o: Identifying a medication contributing to elevated blood pressure
Identifying a medication providing an antihypertensive effect
Identifying a medication replacing repeated blood pressure measurements
Identifying a medication making standing blood pressure measurement unnecessary
explanation:
**Medication review** is part of evaluating potentially reversible contributors to hypertension. Hazzard includes nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs among implicated medications and separately requires appropriate repeated and positional blood pressure measurements (p. 1222). "A complete medication review is warranted to search for medications that may be implicated, for example, corticosteroids and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs including COX-2 inhibitors." (p. 1222).

**A. Identifying a medication contributing to elevated blood pressure.** Correct, the source names nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs among medications that may contribute to elevated pressure (p. 1222).
**B. Identifying a medication providing an antihypertensive effect.** Wrong, in this evaluation, the source identifies this drug class as a possible contributor to elevated pressure, rather than an antihypertensive treatment (p. 1222).
**C. Identifying a medication replacing repeated blood pressure measurements.** Wrong, the source requires repeated measurements for diagnosis; identifying a medication does not satisfy that measurement requirement (p. 1222).
**D. Identifying a medication making standing blood pressure measurement unnecessary.** Wrong, supine and upright readings assess a postural decrease in pressure, an assessment still required in the source (p. 1222).

Source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1222.

q: A 78-year-old man has recovered from pneumonia. Repeated clinic and home blood pressure readings are around 170/90 mm Hg, without orthostatic hypotension. He has untreated stage 2 hypertension and no coronary disease or heart failure. Combination treatment is planned. Which initial regimen best fits the Hazzard approach?
o: A thiazide plus an ACE inhibitor, starting low and titrating gradually
A thiazide plus a beta-blocker, starting low and titrating gradually
A thiazide plus a centrally acting drug, starting low and titrating gradually
A thiazide plus a direct vasodilator, starting low and titrating gradually
explanation:
**Stage 2 hypertension** generally requires combination treatment. Hazzard states: "two antihypertensives should be initiated at the outset" and gives a thiazide with an ACE inhibitor as an example of a synergistic combination (p. 1225). Older patients should start at reduced doses with gradual titration (p. 1225).

**A. A thiazide plus an ACE inhibitor, starting low and titrating gradually.** Correct, the source identifies this combination as an example of complementary therapy and recommends reduced starting doses and gradual titration in older patients (p. 1225).
**B. A thiazide plus a beta-blocker, starting low and titrating gradually.** Wrong, without a compelling indication, beta-blockers are not recommended as first-line antihypertensive agents in older patients; none is supplied in this vignette (p. 1225).
**C. A thiazide plus a centrally acting drug, starting low and titrating gradually.** Wrong, centrally acting antihypertensives are best avoided in older patients because of central nervous system sedation (p. 1225).
**D. A thiazide plus a direct vasodilator, starting low and titrating gradually.** Wrong, direct vasodilators are best avoided in older patients because of their association with marked postural hypotension (p. 1225).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1225.

q: An 82-year-old woman with dementia sometimes refuses tablets. After the team adjusts medication administration, she willingly accepts oral treatment. Persistent hypertension requires treatment; a thiazide previously caused hyponatremia, and there is no cardiac indication for a beta-blocker. Renal function and potassium are normal. Which class is the most appropriate initial choice among these options according to Hazzard?
o: A centrally acting antihypertensive such as clonidine
An ACE inhibitor such as lisinopril
A beta-blocker such as metoprolol
A direct vasodilator such as hydralazine
explanation:
**ACE inhibitors** are an initial-treatment option in older adults. The source favors drugs with fewer adverse effects and advises avoiding centrally acting agents and direct vasodilators because of sedation and marked postural hypotension, respectively; beta-blockers are not a first-line choice without a compelling indication (p. 1225).
"ACE inhibitor agents and angiotensin receptor blockers are choices for initial therapy or as second agents in combination with a thiazide-type diuretic." (p. 1225).
"centrally acting antihypertensive medications and direct vasodilators are best avoided in older hypertensive patients" (p. 1225).

**A. A centrally acting antihypertensive such as clonidine.** Wrong, centrally acting drugs are best avoided because of central nervous system sedating effects, making this an unfavorable initial class here (p. 1225).
**B. An ACE inhibitor such as lisinopril.** Correct, this is a listed initial-treatment class; its favorable adverse-effect profile supports its selection among the choices when a thiazide is unsuitable (p. 1225).
**C. A beta-blocker such as metoprolol.** Wrong, the stem supplies no compelling indication, the condition the source requires for choosing this class first in older patients (p. 1225).
**D. A direct vasodilator such as hydralazine.** Wrong, direct vasodilators are associated with marked postural hypotension and are best avoided as a general initial choice in older patients (p. 1225).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1225.

q: A 75-year-old man with hypertension, prediabetes, and BPH takes chlorthalidone 25 mg daily and tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily. His blood pressure is 146/84. He reports dizziness on standing quickly and nocturia four to five times nightly that disrupts sleep. Glucose is 118, potassium 3.4, and creatinine 1.1. When reviewing possible thiazide adverse effects, which strategy follows the principles described in Hazzard?
o: Increase the thiazide dose to reduce its metabolic adverse effects
Maintain the thiazide dose because urinary frequency is unrelated to this class
Maintain the thiazide dose because hypokalemia is unrelated to this class
Reduce thiazide and add an ACE inhibitor for BP control
explanation:
**Thiazide adverse effects** include hypokalemia and urinary frequency. These effects are less common at lower doses, and the chapter describes combining a thiazide with another agent, including an ACE inhibitor, when additional BP control is needed (p. 1225).
"The most common adverse drug events are metabolic abnormalities, especially hypokalemia, as well as hyperuricemia and impaired glucose intolerance; and urinary frequency or incontinence." (p. 1225).
"However, these side effects are quite uncommon at lower doses." (p. 1225).

**A. Increase the thiazide dose to reduce its metabolic adverse effects.** Wrong, the chapter associates fewer adverse effects with lower, rather than higher, thiazide doses (p. 1225).
**B. Maintain the thiazide dose because urinary frequency is unrelated to this class.** Wrong, urinary frequency is explicitly included among thiazide adverse effects and should not be dismissed during medication review (p. 1225).
**C. Maintain the thiazide dose because hypokalemia is unrelated to this class.** Wrong, hypokalemia is one of the metabolic abnormalities specifically identified with this class (p. 1225).
**D. Reduce thiazide and add an ACE inhibitor for BP control.** Correct, this applies the lower-dose adverse-effect principle while retaining a supported combination strategy for BP control; it does not establish the cause of every symptom in this patient (p. 1225).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 1225.

q: A 77-year-old woman presents after a fall and reports a month of dizziness on standing. She takes amlodipine 10 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, and lisinopril 20 mg each morning. Blood pressure is 138/78 supine and 108/68 after three minutes standing; pulse rises from 68 to 74. Potassium is 3.3 and creatinine 1.2. During medication review, which option both removes the thiazide exposure associated with potassium loss and provides potassium replacement?
o: Move all three antihypertensives to bedtime without changing the prescribed drugs
Stop hydrochlorothiazide and provide potassium replacement with repeat monitoring
Reduce all three antihypertensive doses without providing potassium replacement
Replace lisinopril with an ARB while continuing the other prescribed drugs
explanation:
**Thiazide-associated hypokalemia** is a relevant medication concern. Hazzard identifies hypokalemia among common thiazide adverse effects and describes oral potassium replacement with repeat measurements (pp. 1225, 1270). "The most common adverse drug events are metabolic abnormalities, especially hypokalemia" (p. 1225).

**A. Move all three antihypertensives to bedtime without changing the prescribed drugs.** Wrong, changing administration time retains the thiazide exposure and does not provide potassium replacement (pp. 1225, 1270).
**B. Stop hydrochlorothiazide and provide potassium replacement with repeat monitoring.** Correct, this removes the identified thiazide and replaces potassium; repeat measurements are part of the source's replacement approach (pp. 1225, 1270).
**C. Reduce all three antihypertensive doses without providing potassium replacement.** Wrong, dose reduction leaves thiazide exposure in place and does not provide the replacement specified in the question (pp. 1225, 1270).
**D. Replace lisinopril with an ARB while continuing the other prescribed drugs.** Wrong, changing the renin–angiotensin drug retains hydrochlorothiazide and does not provide the specified potassium replacement (pp. 1225, 1270).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1225, 1270.

q: A 79-year-old woman with hypertension has maintained blood pressure below her individual target on stable treatment after successful lifestyle changes. Which approach to reducing treatment does Hazzard describe?
o: Consider maintaining the current dose as routine after lifestyle success
Consider reducing medication without follow-up of the withdrawal period
Consider reducing or withdrawing medication with planned monitoring
Consider increasing medication to maintain the gains from lifestyle changes
explanation:
**Treatment reassessment** remains appropriate after blood pressure reaches its target on stable therapy. Hazzard describes "a dosage reduction or medication discontinuation during a carefully monitored withdrawal period" especially after successful lifestyle changes (p. 1224).

**A. Consider maintaining the current dose as routine after lifestyle success.** Wrong, routine continuation without reassessment misses the recommendation to periodically reassess the need for ongoing treatment after stabilization (p. 1224).
**B. Consider reducing medication without follow-up of the withdrawal period.** Wrong, the described withdrawal period is carefully monitored; omitting follow-up removes that condition (p. 1224).
**C. Consider reducing or withdrawing medication with planned monitoring.** Correct, stable control and successful lifestyle changes fit the setting in which monitored reduction or withdrawal is considered (p. 1224).
**D. Consider increasing medication to maintain the gains from lifestyle changes.** Wrong, the described response to successful lifestyle changes is reassessment for possible reduction, not escalation to preserve those gains (p. 1224).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1224.

q: A woman treated for hypertension develops hyponatremia and hypokalemia. Which drug class is linked to this pattern in Hazzard’s table of antihypertensive medications for older adults?
o: Treatment with angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors
Treatment with thiazide-type diuretic medications
Treatment with calcium channel antagonists
Treatment with angiotensin receptor blockers
explanation:
**Thiazide-type diuretics** match the electrolyte pattern identified by the table. Their row lists "Metabolic abnormalities (eg, hypokalemia)" and flags "Hyponatremia" as a situation requiring avoidance or monitoring (Table 79-4, p. 1226). The ACE-inhibitor/angiotensin-receptor-blocker row instead lists hyperkalemia, while the calcium-channel-antagonist row lists an absence of metabolic effects (p. 1226).

**A. Treatment with angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors.** Wrong, the combined ACE-inhibitor/angiotensin-receptor-blocker row lists hyperkalemia, which does not match the low-potassium pattern in this question (p. 1226).
**B. Treatment with thiazide-type diuretic medications.** Correct, the row identifies hypokalemia and flags hyponatremia, matching both abnormalities in the stem (p. 1226).
**C. Treatment with calcium channel antagonists.** Wrong, the table lists an absence of metabolic effects and gives edema, constipation, and heart block as potential disadvantages, rather than the electrolyte pattern asked for (p. 1226).
**D. Treatment with angiotensin receptor blockers.** Wrong, these drugs share the table row listing hyperkalemia with ACE inhibitors; that is the opposite potassium abnormality from the one described (p. 1226).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th edition, pp. 1226.

q: בן 76 הסובל מיתר לחץ דם. מה הטיפול התרופתי המתאים על פי הרקע הרפואי שלו?
o: סוכרת- BETA BLOCKERS
אי ספיקת כליות כרונית - DIURETICS
אי ספיקת לב- CALCIUM CHANNEL BLOCKERS
מצב לאחר אוטם שריר הלב- ANGIOTENSIN COVERTIN ENZYME INHIBITORS
explanation:
For hypertension, drug selection also depends on **comorbid disease**. Coronary disease with hypertension supports considering an ACE inhibitor, and the source describes postinfarction benefit especially with additional risk conditions. These drug-condition pairings are not exclusive rules for every patient (Hazzard 8e, pp. 1143, 1226, 1279).
"Current guidelines suggest consideration of ACE inhibitors in all patients having CHD with depressed ventricular function, diabetes, or hypertension." (p. 1143).

**A. Diabetes — beta-blockers.** Wrong, diabetes alone is not the preferred reason to choose a beta-blocker in the table. The source emphasizes ACE inhibitors or ARBs and notes beta-blockers' metabolic effects; an additional cardiac indication could change the choice (pp. 1226, 1279).
**B. Chronic renal failure — diuretics.** Wrong, treatment in kidney disease also depends on proteinuria and progression risk; the source emphasizes renin-angiotensin system blockade in diabetic nephropathy. Rejection of this pairing is not a blanket prohibition on diuretics in kidney disease (p. 1279; inference about the option's wording).
**C. Heart failure — calcium channel blockers.** Wrong, left ventricular dysfunction appears under conditions requiring avoidance or monitoring in the calcium-channel-blocker row. This broad pairing does not justify choosing the whole class for heart failure (p. 1226).
**D. Previous myocardial infarction — ACE inhibitors.** Correct, previous infarction with hypertension supports considering an ACE inhibitor for secondary prevention, and this is the officially accepted pairing (p. 1143).

Note: The pairings do not specify left ventricular function, proteinuria, fluid overload, or drug subclass. The official ranking must not become blanket prohibitions.

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1143, 1226, 1279.

q: על פי המאמר Time to Clinical Benefit of Intensive Blood Pressure Lowering in Patients 60 Years and Older With Hypertension מאת Chen וחבריו ב- JAMA 2022 מה ההשפעה של איזון אגרסיבי של לחץ הדם על MACE- Major adverse cardiovascular events?
o: לא הוכחה יעילות של איזון אגרסיבי של לחץ הדם במניעת MACE באנשים בני 60 ומעלה
האיזון האגרסיבי מונע אירוע אחד של MACE ל- 100 אנשים בשלוש שנים
איזון אגרסיבי של לחץ הדם מומלץ רק באנשים שתוחלת חייהם המשוערת היא יותר מ- 5 שנים
איזון אגרסיבי של לחץ הדם הוכח רק במטופלים עם סוכרת
explanation:
**Benefit accumulates over time**: treatment harms may occur early, whereas prevention of cardiovascular events emerges later. In Chen's analysis, avoiding one event per 100 treated patients took about three years; life expectancy, individual risk, and tolerability therefore matter (Abstract; Results; Discussion).

**A. Intensive BP control has not shown efficacy in preventing MACE in people aged 60 or older.** Wrong, the pooled analysis showed significantly fewer events with intensive treatment, not an absence of benefit (Results).
**B. Intensive control prevents one MACE per 100 people in three years.** Correct, this approximates the time-to-benefit estimate for the absolute-risk-reduction threshold in Table 2; it does not mean every person obtains the same benefit (Results; Table 2).
**C. Intensive control is recommended only with life expectancy above five years.** Wrong, the authors conclude that it may be appropriate for some older adults with life expectancy above three years; they do not impose a five-year requirement (Abstract; Discussion).
**D. Benefit has been shown only in patients with diabetes.** Wrong, Table 1 includes SPRINT and Cardio-Sis, which enrolled people without diabetes (Table 1).

Source: Chen T et al. Time to Clinical Benefit of Intensive Blood Pressure Lowering in Patients 60 Years and Older With Hypertension. JAMA Intern Med. 2022;182:660–667. doi:10.1001/jamainternmed.2022.1657; Abstract, Results, Tables 1–2, Discussion. The inherited online-PDF locators E1, E4, E6 are replaced here by the verified article-section locators.
ref: Time to Clinical Benefit — JAMA, June 2022

q: בת 84, ברקע יתר לחץ דם ואוסטראוארטריטיס. עשתה בדיקת דם שגרתית במרפאה. בבדיקה נמצאה רמת אשלגן 6.4. מה מהווה סיבה אפשרית להיפרקלמיה באשה זו?
o: PRIMARY HYPERALDOSTERONISM
THROMBOCYTOSIS
HYPOMAGNESEMIA
POLYDYPSIA
explanation:
Official answer: ב

**An elevated potassium measurement need not represent true hyperkalemia**. Hazzard lists severe thrombocytosis as a cause of a spurious result and recommends plasma potassium measurement when this is suspected. This distinguishes a sample-related result from a physiologic potassium excess (p. 1271).

**A. Primary hyperaldosteronism.** Wrong, aldosterone excess increases renal potassium excretion and is associated with hypokalemia, so it does not ordinarily explain a high potassium result (pp. 1532–1533).
**B. Thrombocytosis.** Correct, severe thrombocytosis can spuriously elevate measured potassium. The option concerns the measurement and does not necessarily imply excessive body potassium (p. 1271).
**C. Hypomagnesemia.** Wrong, magnesium deficiency impairs renal potassium conservation and is associated with potassium depletion, not the isolated elevation described (Disorders of Magnesium Metabolism, Hypokalemia).
**D. Polydipsia.** Wrong, excessive water intake is primarily associated with hyponatremia. As an inference from that mechanism, it does not explain the thrombocytosis-related spurious potassium elevation (Sailer et al., 2017, Abstract).

Source-to-key note: Severe thrombocytosis, specimen hemolysis and severe leukocytosis can raise measured potassium spuriously. If suspected, the source recommends checking plasma potassium (p. 1271).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1271, 1532–1533; Disorders of Magnesium Metabolism. EJIFCC. 1999;11(2):36–44, Hypokalemia, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6357249/ (no author listed in the cited record); Sailer, Winzeler and Christ-Crain. Primary polydipsia in the medical and psychiatric patient. Swiss Medical Weekly. 2017;147:w14514, Abstract, doi:10.4414/smw.2017.14514.

q: בת 75, עצמאית ב- BADL וללא חסר קוגניטיבי. ברקע אוסטאופורוזיס, מטופלת בוויטמין D ו- ALENDRONATE. בנוסף יתר לחץ דם, שבחצי שנה האחרונה טופל עם דיאטה ופעילות גופנית, ללא טיפול תרופתי. בשבועות האחרונים מספר מדידות של לחץ דם סביב 165/90. מה הגישה הטיפולית הנכונה בחולה זו?
o: המטופלת עם סיכון קרדיו-וסקולרי נמוך ולכן אינה זקוקה לטיפול להורדת לחץ דם
בגילה היעד להורדת לחץ הדם הסיסטולי הינו מתחת ל- 120 mmHg
אוסטאופורוזיס הינו התוויית נגד לטיפול ב-Hydrochlorothiazide
ככל הנראה תזדקק לשתי תרופות להורדת לחץ הדם
explanation:
Persistent **hypertension** at 165/90 in this 75-year-old warrants medication after the unsuccessful lifestyle measures described in the stem (pp. 1223-1225).

**A. Low cardiovascular risk means no blood-pressure treatment is needed.** Wrong, the book describes established treatment benefit in older adults. Persistently elevated pressure despite lifestyle change does not support withholding treatment on that basis (pp. 1223-1225).
**B. Her age sets a systolic target below 120 mmHg.** Wrong, age alone does not define a uniform target; consider comorbidity, tolerability and standing pressure. The intensive-treatment qualification below remains relevant (p. 1223).
**C. Osteoporosis contraindicates hydrochlorothiazide.** Wrong, improved bone mineral density is listed as a thiazide advantage, not an osteoporosis contraindication (p. 1226).
**D. She will probably need two antihypertensive drugs.** Correct, the book states that stage 2 hypertension is likely to require at least two drugs. The persistent systolic pressure fits combination treatment with cautious initiation and titration (p. 1225).

The age-based target statement is wrong because there is no uniform target determined by age alone. The source describes benefit from an SBP target below 120 in selected high-risk older adults and gives a target of 130 for ambulatory community-dwelling older adults, adjusted for tolerability and orthostatic hypotension (Hazzard 8e, pp. 1223-1225).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1223-1226.
